name: model-view-presenter
intent: Separate a screen's presentation logic from its widgets by putting every decision in a presenter that drives a passive view through a narrow view interface, so the screen's behaviour can be tested without the UI toolkit.
problem: Screen behaviour is trapped in widgets and framework event callbacks: the same validation, formatting and navigation logic is duplicated across screens, it can only be exercised by driving the real UI, and swapping a widget or a toolkit breaks behaviour that was never about pixels. The recurring decision is that the view should be a passive interface which the presenter drives.
context: Retained-widget UI stacks (WinForms/WPF, Swing/JavaFX, Qt/GTK, UIKit, ASP.NET Web Forms, Android views) where widgets are objects the presenter can address by method, where automated UI testing is expensive or unavailable in CI, and where the same presentation behaviour must run against several front ends - or against a test double. Also chosen when a team wants explicit, readable control flow instead of implicit data-binding or observer wiring.
benefits: Presentation logic becomes testable without the UI toolkit: the presenter runs against a hand-written view double, so validation, formatting and interaction rules are covered by fast unit tests.
Widget code shrinks to wiring: the view implements one narrow interface, forwards gestures and renders what it is told - no branching on domain state inside event handlers.
One presenter can drive several views (desktop screen, web view, test double, headless export), so presentation behaviour is reused instead of reimplemented per front end.

The view contract is explicit and reviewable: the interface lists exactly what the screen can display and which gestures it reports, which puts the screen's behaviour into one file instead of many handlers.
Separation of concerns is enforced by construction: domain rules stay in the model, display decisions in the presenter, widget mechanics in the view; none of the three needs the others' frameworks.

Explicit flow: presenter methods are ordinary calls, so behaviour is easier to follow, log and debug than implicit observer or data-binding chains (Fowler notes Passive View is the most explicit MVC-family variant).
tradeoffs: Every view update is a manual call: the presenter must push each changed value to the view, so a forgotten call leaves stale widgets on screen - unlike data binding there is no synchronisation safety net.
More code per screen: an interface, a presenter and the wiring between them exist mainly to make the logic testable; small dialogs and simple CRUD screens pay disproportionately for the extra layer.

The presenter is closely coupled to its screen: in the Supervising Controller form it must know which widget shows what and step in for complex effects, which limits reuse across differently shaped screens.

The view itself stays untested: a view double proves the presenter's logic but not the widget wiring, so the pattern shifts rather than removes UI testing effort (Fowler: the view becomes a 'dumb slave').

Lifecycle bookkeeping is mandatory: view and presenter reference each other, so screen recreation (Android rotation, dialog reopen, web re-render) requires explicit detach/re-attach or listeners and frames leak.
Threading becomes a presenter concern: work executed off the UI thread must marshal each view update back to it, an extra contract that the view interface has to document.
Mismatch with modern toolkits: where declarative binding or state-driven rendering exists (WPF bindings, SwiftUI, Compose, React), MVVM/MVI obtain the same separation with less manual update code.

participants.responsibility: The domain or session data the screen presents and edits; the presenter reads and updates it, the view never touches it directly.

Owns the screen's presentation logic: receives gestures from the view, reads and updates the model, formats values for display and pushes every display change back through the view interface. Knows the screen's semantics, no widget class.

The passive contract the presenter drives: semantic operations that display or query screen state (showTotal, selectedStation, showValidationError) plus the gesture entry points the concrete view forwards.

The actual screen or control tree (form, activity, view controller, window) implementing the interface; converts widget events into calls on the presenter, renders exactly what the presenter asks, and holds no application logic.
A stub, fake or mock implementing the same interface used to exercise the presenter without any UI framework; records the calls the presenter made and answers queries on request.

use_cases: Enterprise forms over WinForms, WPF, Swing or JavaFX where validation and formatting logic must be covered by fast tests instead of automation of the real window.

Cross-front-end products: one presenter serving a desktop screen, a web view and a headless test double - Microsoft's MVP documentation used the same model and presenter for ASP.NET Web Forms and WinForms.

Android screens from the pre-ViewModel era: an Activity or Fragment implementing a view interface while a plain presenter holds the logic, so the logic survives configuration changes and process recreation.
Server-side component UIs (ASP.NET Web Forms, GWT, Vaadin) where the generated markup is the passive view and the presenter runs on the server, keeping browser-specific code thin.
Legacy UI rescue: extracting behaviour from event handlers into presenters to make an existing screen testable before a migration or toolkit replacement.
Screens with several interchangeable presentations of one behaviour - phone and tablet layouts, read-only and editing forms, or an export view - all driven by the same presenter.

Google Web Toolkit's official Activities and Places MVP guidance uses interface-defined views, UI-free Activities and a ClientFactory to support multiple implementations and lightweight presenter tests.

Vaadin's Advanced Application Architectures documentation demonstrates a Calculator with a framework-agnostic presenter, a view interface and a Vaadin view implementation, making the pattern concrete for server-side component UIs.

Microsoft's Northwind customer sample applies MVP to ASP.NET Web Forms and Windows Forms: a presenter depends on a view interface and service, with mocks exercising initialization and display behavior outside the UI runtime.
avoid_when: The toolkit already provides the separation declaratively - SwiftUI, Compose, React or WPF-style bindings turn the view into a function of state, and MVVM or MVI expresses that with less manual update code.
A small form whose logic is trivial: direct widget code (or the framework's own MVC) is shorter, and the interface plus presenter would only forward calls.
Screens that merely bind fields to a record: a data-binding setup or a form generator covers it without a presenter.
The team cannot maintain the interface plus view-double discipline: without tests exercising the presenter through the double, the extra layer is pure cost.
Continuous, per-frame UIs (games, drawing tools, data visualisation) where screen state is not a discrete form but a render loop; immediate-mode or scene-graph designs own that interaction.
anti_patterns: Fat view: validation, formatting and navigation drift back into widget event handlers, so the presenter becomes a thin forwarder and the screen is untestable again.
God presenter: one presenter for the whole application (or one per widget) instead of one per screen, accumulating unrelated state and dependencies.
Widget-level view interface: methods such as setLabelText/getTextBox expose the concrete control tree, so the presenter still depends on the UI structure and reuse across front ends dies.
No view double: tests instantiate the real window, reintroducing exactly the framework dependency the pattern was adopted to remove.
Presenter reaching past the screen: talking to the database, remote services or other screens directly instead of going through the model/application layer for this screen's use case.
Bidirectional wiring: the view calls the presenter from every setter and the presenter calls the view back, so update loops and re-entrancy bugs replace a one-way, readable flow.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: display mechanics in the view, presentation logic in the presenter, domain rules in the model.
Dependency inversion: the presenter depends on the view abstraction and is given the concrete view by its owner; it never constructs or looks up widgets.
Single responsibility: one presenter owns one screen's behaviour; the view only renders and forwards.
Information hiding: the view hides its widget structure behind semantic operations, the presenter hides the toolkit from the model and the tests.
Humble object: keep the framework-bound view so thin that not testing it is acceptable (Feathers/Meszaros).
Explicit over implicit: direct presenter calls instead of observer or binding indirection make the screen's flow readable in one place.
best_practices: Define the view interface in presentation vocabulary (showStation, selectedDate, confirmDelete) and never let widgets, controls or toolkit types cross it.
Let the concrete view do nothing but render and forward: no branching on domain state, no formatting decisions, no model access.
Inject view and model into the presenter, keep framework imports out of it, and never let it construct widgets.
Exercise the presenter through a hand-written view double in every test, and keep one integration test for the real view's wiring.
Keep one presenter per screen or use case; split rather than let a presenter accumulate unrelated dependencies.
Detach the view when the screen is destroyed or recreated (Android onDestroy, dispose, disconnect); re-attach to the new view instance explicitly.
Deliver view updates on the UI thread: document which presenter methods may be called from background work and marshal accordingly.

Choose deliberately: Passive View when the logic is complex and the toolkit is hard to test, Supervising Controller when the toolkit's binding covers routine field mapping and only complex effects need the presenter.
sources: Potel, M., 'MVP: Model-View-Presenter - The Taligent Programming Model for C++ and Java', Taligent/IBM (1996) - origin of the pattern: presenter as the generalized controller that interprets events and maps them onto model commands, http://www.wildcrest.com/Potel/Portfolio/mvp.pdf
Fowler, M., GUI Architectures (martinfowler.com, 2006) - MVP's history from Taligent and its relationship to MVC and the Humble View idea, https://martinfowler.com/eaaDev/uiArchs.html

Fowler, M., Passive View (martinfowler.com, 2006) - the view as a dumb slave of the controller, the testability driver and the view-as-Gateway/test-double technique, https://martinfowler.com/eaaDev/PassiveScreen.html

Fowler, M., Supervising Controller (martinfowler.com, 2006) - the variant that leaves simple view/model mapping to data binding and only intervenes for complex view logic, https://martinfowler.com/eaaDev/SupervisingPresenter.html

Wikipedia, 'Model-view-presenter' - history (Taligent, Potel, Dolphin Smalltalk, .NET adoption) and per-platform implementation notes, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model%E2%80%93view%E2%80%93presenter

Google Web Toolkit, 'MVP Activities and Places' - interface-defined views, UI-free Activities, multiple view implementations and lightweight testing in the official GWT framework guide, https://www.gwtproject.org/doc/latest/DevGuideMvpActivitiesAndPlaces.html

Vaadin Docs, 'Advanced Application Architectures' - official Vaadin MVP example with CalculatorModel, CalculatorView and an implementation-agnostic CalculatorPresenter, https://vaadin.com/docs/v8/framework/advanced/advanced-architecture

Microsoft Learn, 'Design Patterns: Model View Presenter' - Northwind sample for ASP.NET Web Forms and Windows Forms with interface-driven presenters and isolated tests, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/archive/msdn-magazine/2006/august/design-patterns-model-view-presenter

Vaadin, 'Is MVP a Best Practice?' - criticism of rigid or over-engineered MVP and guidance to adopt it incrementally when the separation and testability justify the cost, https://vaadin.com/blog/is-mvp-a-best-practice-
